title: Sensitive Query Throttling & Minimization: Vendor Guidance (working draft)
content:
Purpose:
This working draft provides a concise set of contractual and operational guidance Redwood can propose to vendors (managed inference hosts, embedding providers, model brokers) to reduce the risk of sensitive data exposure via inference queries. It blends privacy minimization principles with realistic runtime controls (throttling, sampling, redaction, ephemeral caching).

Scope:
Applies to any third-party endpoint that: (1) receives free-format customer queries for inference, (2) performs model-serving, feature extraction, or caching of request/response artifacts, and (3) stores telemetry or operational logs outside Redwood-managed systems.

High-level objectives:
- Reduce retention of potentially sensitive inputs and outputs.
- Prevent bulk-exfiltration and high-frequency probing of customer data.
- Ensure evidentiary telemetry for audits without keeping raw sensitive payloads longer than necessary.
- Provide clear contractual commitments and an actionable operational playbook.

Key definitions (working):
- Sensitive Query: any request containing PII, credentials, health/financial data, or proprietary code. Parties may use the customer’s data classification mapping.
- Query Throttling: rate-limiting mechanisms (per-user, per-customer, per-API-key) that slow or block excessive request patterns.
- Minimization Controls: techniques (redaction, tokenization, contextual truncation) applied at ingress to avoid storing sensitive content.
- Ephemeral Telemetry: aggregated signals or sampled logs that cannot be reconstructed into original inputs.

Recommended contractual language (short clauses to propose to vendors):
1) Minimization and Retention: Vendor shall not persist raw request payloads containing Sensitive Queries beyond 72 hours unless required for troubleshooting or legal obligation. Any such retention must be documented, justified, and approved by Redwood in writing.

2) Throttling & Abuse Protection: Vendor shall implement per-customer and per-API-key rate limits configurable by Redwood. Vendor must surface the current throttling policy via an API and permit Redwood to request emergency throttling adjustments within 15 minutes.

3) Redaction-on-Ingest: Vendor shall apply customer-configurable redaction rules at ingestion (blacklist/regex/email/ssn patterns, credit-card heuristics, and structured form hooks) and store only redacted payloads for observability. Redaction rules shall be reversible only via secure, auditable processes controlled by Redwood when required for incident response.

4) Ephemeral Telemetry & Sampling: Operational logs provided to Redwood must use deterministic sampling of payloads and be stored in an irrecoverable hashed or tokenized form when containing excerpts of user inputs. Any full payload snapshots retained for debugging require explicit pre-approved exceptions and must be procedurally erased after remediation.

5) Audit & Evidence: Vendor shall maintain tamper-evident audit trails for any access to sensitive payloads or reversal operations and shall produce evidence within 5 business days upon Redwood request.

6) Security Incidents: Vendor must notify Redwood within 12 hours of detecting possible exfiltration or policy violations involving Sensitive Queries, provide a containment plan, and retain all relevant telemetry untouched for forensics for minimum 30 days.

Operational controls (implementation guidance):
- Default deny: New tenant/API keys should start with conservative per-minute and per-hour caps; allow Redwood to escalate based on stable usage metrics.
- Adaptive throttling: Use anomaly detection on rate, token patterns, and schema variance to automatically escalate throttles for suspicious behavior (e.g., repeated pattern-based probing).
- Burst windows: Allow short, bounded bursts with cumulative daily caps to support real customer spikes while preventing continuous scraping.
- Ingress sanitizers: Provide pipeline hooks for regex-based redaction, form-binding identification, and named-entity detection (NER) filters to avoid storing PII unnecessarily.
- KV/Prefix cache handling: Ensure cached KV segments with user-provided context have per-tenant TTLs and are wiped on deprovisioning. Do not write raw KV payloads to long-term logs.

Telemetry & evidence design: what Redwood needs to see (without raw payloads):
- Aggregated metrics: per-tenant request counts, token distribution, throttled request counts, anomalous IPs.
- Sampling records: list of sampled request ids (hashed), sampling probability, reason code for sample (debug, incident, random).
- Access logs: who accessed which sampled artifact and why (with justification tag).
- Redaction audit: redaction rule id + fingerprint, number of redactions applied, reversible-flag if reversal used and by whom.

Sample SLA table (for redlines) - short form to include in attachments: 
- Notification of suspected exfiltration: 12 hours
- Emergency throttling request response: 15 minutes
- Evidence delivery (for valid audit): 5 business days
- Proof of deletion after approved retention: 3 business days

Exception handling & approved debug windows:
- Vendors may request a debug exception for retention >72 hours; requests must include business justification, TTL, and narrow scoping. Approvals are time-limited and recorded.
- All exception operations must be tagged and auditable.

Suggested minimal technical controls checklist (quick):
- [ ] Per-API-key and per-tenant rate limiting (configurable by Redwood)
- [ ] Ingest redaction pipeline with pattern library and NER integration
- [ ] Ephemeral storage TTLs for request payloads <= 72 hours by default
- [ ] Deterministic sampling mechanism and hashed sample identifiers
- [ ] Tamper-evident audit trails for reversal/unredaction operations
- [ ] Emergency throttling API for Redwood with documented SLA

Legal drafting notes / negotiation strategy (internal):
- Be pragmatic: vendors will push back on strict short retention windows if they need payloads to train models or improve quality. Push for narrow scoped exceptions only and strong auditability.
- Offer a transition path: shorter retention in production, longer retention during a limited onboarding window while metrics stabilize.
- Reserve audit rights and forensic access in contracts; these are high-value concessions for customers and regulators.

Open questions / TODOs (please comment inline):
- Should 72h be default for all vendors or tiered (SMB vs. enterprise)? pros/cons.
- How to handle vendor-side model improvement requests that require sample inputs? Proposed answer: hashed sample pointers + opt-in export process per customer with documented consent.
- Integration work: define the minimal API for emergency throttling (proto spec). Owner: Marcus Chen.

Appendix: Example short redline clause for SOC/Procurement teams to paste into vendor agreements:
"Vendor shall apply customer-configurable minimization controls to all customer-supplied inference inputs. Raw input payloads containing Sensitive Queries shall not be retained beyond seventy-two (72) hours except where (a) required for imminent incident remediation and approved in writing by Customer, or (b) retention is necessary to comply with law, in which case Vendor shall notify Customer promptly and provide custodian evidence as set forth in this Agreement."

Working notes / tone: this doc is intentionally prescriptive but pragmatic — aim is to produce a clause set that legal and procurement can use in early vendor conversations and that SRE/infra can implement with clear SLAs.

Last edited by: Sofia Martinez (sec-compliance).
